chem_ocra.1.1.summary: These revision notes provide a comprehensive, Grade 9 level breakdown of the nuclear atom and the typical sizes of atoms and small molecules for OCR GCSE Chemistry. They explore the central, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by orbiting electrons in a vast empty space. Additionally, they detail the microscopic scale of atomic dimensions and how to convert standard form values for exam success.

core.p: Atoms are the basic building blocks of all matter in the universe. In modern chemistry, the structure of an atom is described as a nuclear model, featuring a tiny, dense core surrounded by vast empty space.
bullets: Every atom consists of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons.
The nucleus is surrounded by electrons that move rapidly in the space outside it.
The vast majority of an atom's volume is completely empty space.
Almost all of the mass of an atom is concentrated in its tiny nucleus.

callouts.p: The model of the atom with a positive nucleus and electrons orbiting in the empty space around it.

core.p: The nucleus sits directly at the absolute center of every atom. It is extremely small compared to the overall size of the atom yet holds nearly all of its mass.
bullets: Contains positively charged particles called protons.
Contains neutral particles called neutrons (except in standard hydrogen-1).
Collectively, protons and neutrons in the nucleus are referred to as nucleons.
Bound together by strong nuclear forces, overcoming the electrostatic repulsion between positive protons.

callouts.p: The central part of an atom containing protons and neutrons.

fig.cap: Diagram showing a zoomed-in central atomic nucleus containing protons and neutrons.

core.p: Electrons are extremely light, negatively charged subatomic particles that exist outside the nucleus. They occupy specific energy levels or shells at relatively huge distances from the nucleus.
bullets: Carry a negative relative charge of -1.
Have a negligible mass (approx 1/1836 of a proton).
Orbit or exist within electrostatic attraction bounds around the positive nucleus.
Account for the chemical reactivity of the atom based on their arrangement.

callouts.p: In GCSE calculations, electron mass is treated as zero because it is so small compared to protons and neutrons.

core.p: Atoms are unimaginably small. Understanding their typical dimensions requires standard form and nanometres, as human eyes cannot detect individual atoms.
bullets: The typical radius of a single atom is about 0.1 nanometres (nm).
In standard form, an atomic radius is approximately 1 x 10^-10 metres.
One nanometre is equal to 1 x 10^-9 metres.
Different elements have slightly different atomic radii, increasing down a group.

callouts.p: Learn the value 0.1 nm or 1 x 10^-10 m as the typical radius of an atom for exam questions.

fig.cap: Visualising an atom showing the outer electron cloud and the tiny central nucleus.

core.h: 5. Scale and Size of the Nucleus
core.p: While the atom itself is tiny, the nucleus inside it is on an entirely different scale of microscopic proportions, being tens of thousands of times smaller than the atom.
bullets: The radius of a nucleus is typically about 1 x 10^-14 metres.
This is roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller than the radius of the whole atom.
If an atom were the size of a large sports stadium, the nucleus would only be the size of a marble on the center spot.
Because of this extreme size difference, almost all of the atom is empty space.

callouts.p: Do not confuse the size of the atom (10^-10 m) with the size of the nucleus (10^-14 m). The difference is factor of 10,000.

core.p: Small molecules consist of a fixed number of atoms covalently bonded together. Their overall sizes are slightly larger than individual atoms, though still measured in nanometres.
bullets: Small molecules like water (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), and oxygen (O2) have dimensions typically between 0.1 nm and a few nanometres.
The size depends directly on the number of atoms bonded together and their atomic radii.
Simple molecular substances consist of these distinct small molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them.
Molecules like buckminsterfullerene (C60) are larger nanostructures, around 1 nm in diameter.

callouts.p: Small molecules are also on the nanometre scale, typically spanning fractions of a nanometre up to a few nanometres.

core.p: A profound realization in modern chemistry and physics is that solid matter is fundamentally composed of mostly empty space.
bullets: Electrons occupy energy levels far from the tiny central nucleus.
Because the nucleus is 10,000 times smaller than the atom, the volume ratio means over 99.999999% of an atom is empty space.
The apparent solidity of macroscopic objects is due to electrostatic repulsion between the outer electrons of colliding atoms, not physical touching of nuclei.

callouts.p: Always state that 'most of the mass is in the nucleus' and 'most of the volume is empty space' when describing atomic structure.

core.p: A direct comparison of mass and radius across subatomic particles, nuclei, and atoms clarifies why certain approximations are valid in GCSE chemistry.
bullets: Proton/Neutron radius: much smaller than nuclear radius, effectively fundamental point-like particles at this level.
Electron: orbits at great distances, defining the overall boundary and volume of the atom.
Mass concentration: over 99.9% of mass resides in nucleons weighing approx 1 atomic mass unit each.

core.h: 9. Historical Context: The Nuclear Model Discovery
core.p: The understanding that atoms have a central nucleus came from the famous alpha particle scattering experiment conducted by Ernest Rutherford, Geiger, and Marsden.
bullets: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed straight through, proving atoms are mostly empty space.
A very small number of alpha particles were deflected at large angles.
An even smaller fraction bounced straight back, proving the existence of a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
This disproved the earlier 'plum pudding' model where positive charge and mass were spread evenly.

callouts.p: Straight-through passage = empty space; deflection = positive nucleus containing almost all mass.

fig.cap: Simplified alpha scattering showing most particles passing through and few deflecting off the dense nucleus.

core.h: 10. Standard Form Conversion for Atomic Sizes
core.p: Exams frequently test your ability to convert between nanometres, metres, and standard form when comparing atomic dimensions.
bullets: To convert from nm to m, multiply by 10^-9.
To find how many atoms fit across a distance, divide the total distance by the diameter of one atom.
Always check units carefully before performing calculations.

callouts.p: Practice entering standard form numbers like 1 x 10^-10 into your calculator using the EXP or x10^x button rather than typing multiplication manually.

analogy.p:
Imagine an entire atom is scaled up to the size of a massive professional football stadium. On this colossal scale, the central nucleus would be roughly the size of a single marble resting right on the center spot. The electrons would be like tiny gnats buzzing around the very highest rows of the seating stands. Everything in between—the entire expanse of the seating bowl and pitch—is completely empty space. This accurately illustrates why atoms are mostly empty space and why mass is concentrated in the tiny center.

Where the analogy breaks down: In reality, electrons do not behave like solid little bugs buzzing on a fixed flight path; they exist as a quantum electron cloud with probabilities of being found in certain regions. Furthermore, nuclei are not solid marbles made of a uniform substance, but tight clusters of distinct nucleons interacting via quantum forces.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element that can exist, consisting of a central nucleus surrounded by electrons.
The tiny, dense, positively charged central core of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A subatomic particle found in the nucleus with a relative charge of +1 and a relative mass of 1.
A neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus with a relative charge of 0 and a relative mass of 1.
A subatomic particle orbiting the nucleus with a relative charge of -1 and negligible mass.
The typical distance from the center of the nucleus to the outer boundary of the electron cloud, approx 0.1 nm.
A unit of length equal to 10^-9 metres (one billionth of a metre).
A way of writing very large or very small numbers as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.
The scientific model of the atom featuring a central nucleus and orbiting electrons.
The vast volume of the atom outside the nucleus where electrons are located.
A particle made of a small, fixed number of atoms joined by covalent bonds, typically on the nanometre scale.
A generic term for a subatomic particle located in the nucleus (either a proton or a neutron).

mistakes.w: Saying the atom is solid throughout.
mistakes.r: Atoms consist of mostly empty space, with a tiny dense nucleus and distant electrons.

mistakes.w: Confusing atomic radius size (10^-10 m) with nuclear radius size (10^-14 m).
mistakes.r: The nuclear radius is 10,000 times smaller than the atomic radius.

mistakes.w: Stating that electrons are found inside the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Electrons orbit in the space outside the nucleus; only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Writing that molecules are larger than cells or visible particles.
mistakes.r: Small molecules are measured in nanometres (10^-9 m) and are sub-microscopic.

mistakes.w: Forgetting standard form units when stating atomic size.
mistakes.r: Always include units such as metres (m) or nanometres (nm).

mistakes.w: Believing neutrons have a positive or negative charge.
mistakes.r: Neutrons are neutral with a charge of 0.

mistakes.w: Stating that the mass of an atom is spread evenly.
mistakes.r: Almost all of the mass is concentrated in the tiny nucleus.

exam.q: State the approximate radius of a typical atom.
exam.tip: Learn this exact number as it is a frequent direct recall question.

exam.q: Describe the distribution of mass and volume within an atom.
model: Almost all the mass is concentrated in the nucleus
Most of the volume of the atom is empty space
exam.tip: Make sure to contrast mass (nucleus) with volume (empty space) clearly.

exam.q: Compare the size of an atom's nucleus with the size of the whole atom.
model: The nucleus is much smaller than the atom
The radius of the nucleus is about 10,000 times smaller (or roughly 1 x 10^-14 m compared to 1 x 10^-10 m)
exam.tip: Use a factor of 10,000 or cite the respective standard form radii.

exam.q: Name the two types of subatomic particles found in the nucleus of an atom.
model: Protons
Neutrons
exam.tip: Do not include electrons here; they are outside the nucleus.

exam.q: Explain why most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil in Rutherford's experiment.
model: Atoms are composed of mostly empty space
Therefore alpha particles did not hit anything and passed straight through
exam.tip: Link the experimental observation directly to the presence of empty space.

exam.q: Convert 0.05 nanometres into metres in standard form.
model: Correct standard form format
exam.tip: Remember shifting the decimal point changes the power of 10 accordingly.

exam.q: State where electrons are located in the nuclear model of the atom.
model: In the space outside the nucleus (in energy levels/shells)

exam.q: Explain what subatomic particles determine the mass of an atom and where they are located.
model: Protons and neutrons determine the mass
Electrons have negligible mass
They are located in the nucleus
exam.tip: Award points for naming particles, mentioning negligible electron mass, and locating them.

exam.q: What is the typical size range of a small molecule?
model: Around 0.1 nm to a few nanometres (or 10^-10 m order of magnitude)
exam.tip: Relate molecule size to atomic size since molecules are made of bonded atoms.

worked.q: Calculate how many gold atoms can fit side-by-side along a straight line 1 cm long, given that the radius of a gold atom is 0.14 nm.
steps: Find the diameter of one gold atom: 0.14 nm x 2 = 0.28 nm.
Convert the diameter into metres: 0.28 x 10^-9 m = 2.8 x 10^-10 m.
Convert the total distance (1 cm) into metres: 1 cm = 0.01 m = 1 x 10^-2 m.
Divide total distance by atomic diameter: (1 x 10^-2 m) / (2.8 x 10^-10 m) = 3.57 x 10^7 atoms.

worked.q: The radius of a carbon atom is 0.070 nm and the radius of its nucleus is 2.7 x 10^-15 m. Calculate the ratio of the atom's radius to the nucleus's radius.
steps: Convert carbon atom radius into metres: 0.070 nm = 0.070 x 10^-9 m = 7.0 x 10^-11 m.
Identify the nuclear radius in metres: 2.7 x 10^-15 m.
Divide atomic radius by nuclear radius: (7.0 x 10^-11) / (2.7 x 10^-15).
Calculate the final ratio value: 25,925 (or approx 2.6 x 10^4).

chem_ocra.1.0.summary: The atomic model has evolved significantly over the past two centuries as new experimental evidence emerged from various scientists. Starting from indivisible solid spheres, the model progressed through the discovery of electrons and the nuclear model, culminating in quantum and neutron-based refinements. Understanding this historical progression demonstrates how scientific theories are constantly tested, challenged, and modified when new data cannot be explained by existing models.

core.h: 1. Ancient Greek and Early Solid Sphere Model
core.p: Before modern scientific experimentation, ancient philosophers debated the fundamental nature of matter. John Dalton translated these philosophical ideas into the first scientific atomic theory in the early 19th century, proposing that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible, hard spheres called atoms.
bullets: John Dalton proposed his atomic theory in 1803.
Atoms were described as solid, indivisible spheres, like billiard balls.
All atoms of a given element were stated to be identical in mass and properties.
Atoms of different elements were thought to have different masses and characteristics.
Chemical reactions involved rearranging these unchanging spheres in new combinations.

callouts.p: A solid, indivisible sphere that makes up all chemical elements.
Do not state Dalton's model included subatomic particles; he believed atoms could not be split.

core.p: J.J. Thomson changed our understanding of the atom in 1897 by discovering the electron using cathode ray tubes. This breakthrough proved that atoms were not indivisible solid spheres, as they contained much smaller, negatively charged particles embedded within them.
bullets: Cathode rays were deflected by electric and magnetic fields, proving they were charged.
The charge-to-mass ratio of the rays was independent of the gas or metal used.
This proved the particles existed in all types of matter.
These negative particles were named electrons.

callouts.p: The electron was the first subatomic particle discovered, breaking the rule of indivisibility.

fig.cap: Figure 1: J.J. Thomson's Cathode Ray Tube experiment showing deflection of negative particles.

core.p: Following the discovery of the electron, J.J. Thomson proposed the plum pudding model in 1904. Since atoms are overall neutral, he reasoned that the negatively charged electrons must be embedded in a sea or cloud of positive charge to balance them out.
bullets: The atom is a sphere of positive charge.
Negatively charged electrons are scattered throughout this positive sphere.
Resembles a traditional British Christmas pudding with plums embedded in dough.
Cannot account for large deflections in later scattering experiments.

callouts.p: An atomic model where negative electrons are embedded in a positive sphere.
Think of chocolate chips spread throughout a ball of cookie dough.

fig.cap: Figure 2: The Plum Pudding Model with negative electrons scattered inside a positive sphere.

core.h: 4. Rutherford and the Nuclear Atom Experiment
core.p: Ernest Rutherford, along with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, tested the plum pudding model by firing alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil. The results completely disproved Thomson's model and led to the creation of the nuclear model.
bullets: Alpha particles are heavy, fast-moving, positively charged helium nuclei.
Gold foil was hammered extremely thin, only a few atoms thick.
Most alpha particles passed straight through with zero deflection.
A very small number of particles were deflected by large angles.
About 1 in 8000 particles bounced straight back or deflected >90 degrees.

callouts.p: Must be performed in a vacuum so air molecules do not deflect the alpha particles.

core.h: 5. Conclusions from the Alpha Scattering Experiment
core.p: Rutherford analysed the trajectories of the alpha particles to deduce the internal structure of the atom. The surprising results required a complete redesign of the atomic model because standard electrostatic forces in the plum pudding model could not cause large deflections.
bullets: Most of the atom is empty space, explaining why most alpha particles passed straight through.
The positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense central region called the nucleus.
The mass of the atom is almost entirely concentrated in this nucleus.
Negatively charged electrons orbit the nucleus at a distance.

callouts.p: An atom with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus surrounded by orbiting electrons in empty space.

fig.cap: Figure 3: Alpha particle scattering showing deflection off a dense positive nucleus.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><circle cx="240" cy="120" r="20" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="215" y="90" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Dense Nucleus</text><path d="M 60 80 L 340 80" fill="none" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 60 150 L 190 150 L 320 200" fill="none" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="2"/><text x="70" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#3b82f6">Straight path</text><text x="190" y="190" font-size="12" fill="#ef4444">Deflected path</text></svg>

core.p: Niels Bohr adapted Rutherford's nuclear model in 1913 by performing calculations that showed electrons orbiting at random distances would spiral into the nucleus. He proposed that electrons occupy fixed energy levels or shells at specific distances from the nucleus.
bullets: Electrons cannot occupy any arbitrary position between shells.
Each shell represents a fixed energy level.
Electrons can jump between shells by absorbing or emitting specific amounts of energy (light).
This theoretical model matched experimental atomic emission spectra perfectly.

callouts.p: Bohr's mathematical calculations matched experimental line spectra, proving his shell model correct.

core.p: Further experiments refined the nucleus itself. In 1919, Rutherford discovered positive particles inside the nucleus, naming them protons. Later, in 1932, James Chadwick discovered the neutron, explaining isotopes and resolving discrepancies in atomic mass calculations.
bullets: Protons carry a single positive charge and account for part of the nuclear mass.
The number of protons determines the atomic number (element identity).
Neutrons have no charge (are neutral) and have a mass very similar to protons.
The discovery of the neutron completed the classic three-particle model of the atom.

callouts.p: A neutral subatomic particle located in the nucleus, discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.

core.h: 8. Chronological Summary of the Atomic Models
core.p: Reviewing the historical development shows a clear linear progression where each scientific model was tested and replaced when new empirical evidence failed to fit existing predictions.
bullets: Dalton (1803): Solid indivisible spheres.
Thomson (1897): Plum pudding model (electrons in positive cloud).
Rutherford (1909): Nuclear model (dense central nucleus, empty space).
Bohr (1913): Electron shell model (fixed energy levels).
Chadwick (1932): Neutron discovery (complete modern model).

callouts.p: Examiners frequently ask you to place models in chronological order or explain how one model replaced another.

core.h: 9. How Scientific Models Change over Time
core.p: Scientific understanding is not absolute; models change when new evidence emerges that cannot be explained by the current theory. The shift from the plum pudding model to the nuclear model is a textbook example of the scientific method in action.
bullets: Experimental anomalies drive scientific revolutions.
If a theory cannot explain data, it must be modified or discarded.
Advanced technology (vacuum pumps, radiation sources, computers) enables finer measurements.
Peer review validates new atomic models before scientific consensus is reached.

callouts.p: Scientific models are only as good as the experimental evidence supporting them.

core.h: 10. Comparing Plum Pudding and Nuclear Models
core.p: This table summarises the core structural differences that examiners expect candidates to contrast in exam questions.

head: Feature
Plum Pudding Model
Nuclear Model
rows: Positive charge confined to tiny nucleus
Orbiting at a distance in empty space
Would pass through with tiny deflections
Most pass through, few deflect massively

bullets: Notice how charge and mass shift from diffuse to concentrated.

callouts.p: Do not mix up where electrons are located in Thomson versus Rutherford models.

core.p: While Bohr's model worked exceptionally well for hydrogen, it failed to accurately predict the spectra of multi-electron atoms. Further quantum mechanical refinements were subsequently developed by scientists like Schrödinger and Heisenberg.
bullets: Bohr's model assumed circular orbits for electrons.
Subsequent quantum models use electron clouds and orbitals instead of strict 2D rings.
The fundamental concept of fixed energy levels, however, remains valid and GCSE-approved.

callouts.p: At GCSE OCR, you only need to know Bohr's shells up to element 20 (calcium); true quantum orbitals are A-level content.

core.p: Memorising this timeline is essential for answering multi-mark history of science questions.
bullets: Dates do not need to be memorised down to the exact month, but the sequence must be correct.

callouts.p: Dalton -> Thomson -> Rutherford -> Bohr -> Chadwick.

analogy.t: The Apple and the Sports Stadium Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine an atom is the size of a giant Wembley sports stadium. On this scale, the nucleus is the size of a single marble sitting right on the centre spot, yet it contains almost all the mass of the stadium. The electrons are tiny gnats buzzing around high up in the empty seating rows. This helps explain why most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil with no obstruction—because the atom is almost entirely empty space! Where it breaks down: The marble nucleus and gnat electrons are not actually solid physical objects touching each other like macroscopic items; they are bound by electrostatic and quantum forces.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element that can exist, consisting of a nucleus surrounded by electrons.
An early atomic theory picturing atoms as solid, indivisible spheres.
An atomic model featuring negative electrons embedded in a positive sphere of charge.
The model featuring a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons orbiting outside.
A positively charged particle consisting of two protons and two neutrons (helium nucleus).
The scattering experiment that proved atoms have a dense, positive nucleus.
A fixed energy level at a specific distance from the nucleus where electrons orbit.
The tiny, central core of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus.
A neutrally charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus.
Particles smaller than an atom, namely protons, neutrons, and electrons.
A specific shell or region where electrons can exist around a nucleus.

mistakes.r: Dalton proposed solid spheres; J.J. Thomson discovered electrons.
Alpha particles are positively charged helium nuclei.

mistakes.w: Claiming the plum pudding model has a nucleus.
mistakes.r: The plum pudding model has no nucleus; positive charge is spread evenly.

mistakes.w: Stating electrons are inside the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Electrons orbit outside the nucleus in shells or energy levels.
James Chadwick discovered neutrons in 1932; Rutherford discovered protons.

mistakes.w: Believing atoms are mostly solid mass.
Confusing Bohr shells with Dalton spheres.
mistakes.r: Bohr introduced energy levels within the nuclear model.

exam.q: Describe J.J. Thomson's plum pudding model of the atom.
model: A sphere of positive charge
With negative electrons embedded in it
exam.tip: Mention both the positive sphere and the embedded electrons to secure all marks.

exam.q: Explain why most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil in Rutherford's experiment.
model: Most of the atom is empty space
So the alpha particles did not hit anything and were not deflected
exam.tip: Link the observation directly to empty space.

exam.q: State two ways the nuclear model of the atom is different from the plum pudding model.
model: Nuclear model has a central nucleus; plum pudding does not
Nuclear model has electrons orbiting outside; plum pudding has electrons embedded inside (or mass concentrated in nucleus vs spread out)
exam.tip: Make sure to contrast both models clearly without mixing features.

exam.q: Explain how the results of the alpha scattering experiment led to the development of the nuclear model. (3 marks)
model: Most particles passed straight through, showing the atom is mostly empty space
Some particles were deflected at large angles, showing a concentrated positive charge
A few bounced straight back, showing the nucleus is very dense and contains most of the mass
exam.tip: Break your answer down into observation and conclusion for each point.

exam.q: Who discovered the neutron and in what year approximately?
model: James Chadwick
exam.tip: Remember Chadwick for neutrons, Rutherford for protons/nucleus, Thomson for electrons.

exam.q: Put the following atomic models in chronological order from earliest to most recent: Bohr model, Dalton model, Nuclear model, Plum pudding model.
model: Dalton model -> Plum pudding model -> Nuclear model -> Bohr model
(Award 1 mark if 3 are correct in order)
exam.tip: Learn the sequence: Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr, Chadwick.

exam.q: Explain why Niels Bohr adapted Rutherford's nuclear model.
model: Calculations showed electrons would spiral into the nucleus
Bohr proposed electrons orbit in fixed energy levels or shells at specific distances
exam.tip: Focus on the instability of crashing into the nucleus without fixed shells.

exam.q: State the relative charge and approximate mass of an electron.
model: Charge: -1
Mass: Very small / negligible / 1/1836 (or zero)
exam.tip: Make sure to specify negative charge and near-zero mass.

exam.q: Describe what John Dalton's atomic theory stated about atoms.
model: All matter is made of tiny, indivisible spheres called atoms
Atoms of the same element are identical, while atoms of different elements are different

exam.q: Explain why scientific models of the atom have changed over time.
model: New experimental evidence was discovered
Existing models could not explain the new data, so they were modified or replaced
exam.tip: Always link model changes to new experimental evidence.

worked.q: An alpha particle scattering experiment fires 100,000 alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Estimate how many particles bounce back at angles greater than 90 degrees, and explain why.
steps: Recall experimental statistics: approximately 1 in 8,000 alpha particles are deflected by more than 90 degrees or bounce back.
Explain the reason: A tiny fraction hit the extremely small, dense, positively charged nucleus head-on.
worked.ans: Approximately 12 to 13 particles. This occurs because the nucleus is extremely small and dense, meaning very few alpha particles pass close enough to experience a large enough repulsive positive force to bounce back.

worked.q: Compare the location of mass and charge in Dalton's model versus Rutherford's nuclear model.
steps: Identify Dalton's model properties: Solid sphere, mass and positive/neutral nature spread uniformly throughout the hard ball.
Identify Rutherford's model properties: Mass and positive charge concentrated entirely in a tiny central nucleus, with light electrons orbiting in empty space.
worked.ans: In Dalton's model, mass and charge are spread uniformly throughout a solid, indivisible sphere. In Rutherford's nuclear model, almost all the mass and all the positive charge are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, with electrons occupying empty space outside.
